paper_metadata.title: Quantum Encoding and Analysis on Continuous Time Stochastic Process with Financial Applications

summary: The paper proposes a gate-based QCTSP framework for continuous-time stochastic processes, with explicit resource formulas such as exponential-distribution preparation in ⌈log(-1/λ ln ϵ)⌉ qubits and depth 1, general Lévy preparation in O(S + n log(nS)) depth, and continuous Markov preparation in nS2 depth. It also gives amplitude-estimation-based extraction with O(P + nlxlτ) depth for weightless integrals and O(P + F + nlxlτ + n max(lx, lτ)) or O(P + G + nlYlT) for weighted integrals, plus simulation shot counts of 1024 and 1000 in the option-pricing and ruin-probability examples, respectively.

experiments.description: Quantum continuous-time stochastic process (QCTSP) state preparation and information extraction framework, including evaluation of weighted integrals and history-sensitive first-hitting/ruin-type quantities; demonstrated on Merton jump-diffusion option pricing and collective-risk ruin probability as gate-based quantum circuits and amplitude-estimation subroutines.

algorithm.variant: QCTSP framework with holding-time and increment representations; controlled-rotation Riemann-sum evaluation plus standard amplitude estimation

hyperparameters.truncation_error_epsilon: paper-defined truncation bound for distributions/time support
hyperparameters.Fourier_order_L: used in Fourier approximation for fP,L
hyperparameters.sample_path_steps_n: number of pieces/steps in the CTSP path
hyperparameters.shot_count: 1000 shots in ruin-probability simulation figure; 1024 shots per group in option-pricing simulation figure

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Distribution states prepared via Grover-style state preparation / controlled rotations; jump sizes in the option-pricing simulation were generated by a classical random generator and then implemented on the target qubit

problem_formulation.encoding_details: CTSP encoded into registers for index, data, and time; holding-time representation stores (Xj, tauj), increment representation stores (Yj, Tj). For the option-pricing and ruin-probability applications, path variables are accumulated through adders/subtractors and controlled rotations rather than a QUBO mapping.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Evaluate expectations of functions of path integrals and history-sensitive quantities, including E[f(∫_0^T X(t)dt)], E[f(∫_0^T g(t)X(t)dt)], European call option price under Merton jump diffusion, and ruin probability under the collective risk model.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Flag qubits, controlled subtraction, and post-selection/measurement used to detect first-hitting or ruin events; amplitude estimation used for expectation extraction.
problem_formulation.num_ancilla_qubits: flag qubits and target qubit(s) used; exact ancilla count not fully specified

problem_instance.description: Continuous-time stochastic processes in finance/statistics; explicit applications to Merton jump-diffusion European call option pricing and collective-risk ruin probability.

dataset_specification.description: Synthetic stochastic-process instances parameterized by process rates, jump-size distributions, and financial parameters; no real-market dataset used

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: CTSP discretized into finite pieces; distributions truncated to finite support with error bound epsilon; Fourier approximation used for generic integrable functions
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Simulation figures compare quantum results with Merton formula, Black-Scholes baseline, classical Monte Carlo, and theoretical ruin-probability benchmark; 1024 shots per group for option pricing and 1000 shots per simulation point for ruin probability

implementation_details.classical_solver: classical random generator used for jump sizes in the option-pricing simulation; classical Monte Carlo and analytic formulas used as baselines
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Distribution truncation, Fourier approximation, and classical generation of some random jump sizes in the option-pricing simulation
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Measurement-based estimation of expectation values; comparison against Merton formula, Black-Scholes, classical Monte Carlo, and theoretical ruin-probability curve

speedup_claims.caveats: Asymptotic claim; depends on process class and truncation parameters.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: State preparation: e.g., O(n(S+log(nS))) for general Lévy, O(nS⌈S+log(-ln ε/λmin)⌉) for continuous Markov, and O(n(qF+qG−ln ε/|λmin|)) for Cox. Information extraction: quadratic speedup via amplitude estimation, with O(LP/ε(...)) time complexity for expectation evaluation.
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical Monte Carlo is referenced as the classical counterpart, but no single explicit asymptotic bound is given for the full CTSP framework in the paper text.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not reported; no empirical crossover analysis is given.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: State-preparation formulas and amplitude-estimation-based extraction; no end-to-end resource estimate for a practical advantage demonstration.
limiting_factors: No specific QPU or noisy hardware demonstration
Large state-preparation overheads for general CTSP subclasses
Classical baselines are only used for comparison, not beaten on a meaningful benchmark
Data loading and distribution preparation remain substantial

notes: No gate-based QPU or vendor is named; the paper presents circuit constructions and simulation figures, so hardware.type is inferred as simulator_other.
The paper reports multiple resource formulas rather than one fixed qubit count/depth because the framework covers several CTSP subclasses and two application circuits.
The option-pricing and ruin-probability sections describe simulation results and shot counts, but not a specific backend or transpiled circuit metrics.
The paper presents a theoretical framework and simulation figures, but no practical quantum advantage benchmark over classical methods is demonstrated.

experiments.description: State preparation of a memory-less continuous-time stochastic process holding time, with exponential distribution preparation via parallel RY rotations.
key_results: Holding time follows exponential distribution P[τj ≥ t] = e^{-λjt}.
Prepared with ⌈log(-1/λj ln ϵ)⌉ qubits, circuit depth 1, and gate complexity ⌈log(-1/λj ln ϵ)⌉.

experiments.description: General Lévy-process state preparation using jump, Brownian, and adder subcircuits.
key_results: Prepared on n log(nS) qubits within O(S + n log(nS)) circuit depth.
Prepared on n⌈log(-S/λmin ln ϵ)⌉ qubits.
Circuit depth nS2 and gate complexity O(nS⌈S + log(-ln ϵ/λmin)⌉).

experiments.description: Cox-process state preparation with stochastic intensity and IID increments.
key_results: Prepared on O(n(qF + qG - ln ϵ/|λmin|)) qubits.
Circuit depth O(max{qG, qF + 2dF} + nqG) or O(max{qG, qF + 2dF} - n ln ϵ/λmin) depending on representation.

experiments.description: Weighted-integral extraction for QCTSP using increment or holding-time representations.
key_results: Holding-time representation: circuit depth P + F + nlxlτ + n max(lx, lτ).
Increment representation: circuit depth O(P + G + nlYlT).
Both use Fourier approximation and amplitude estimation.

experiments.description: History-sensitive first-hitting-time / ruin-event extraction using flag qubits and controlled subtraction.
key_results: Uses n flag qubits plus O(log B) bound register.
Detects first hit via controlled subtraction and CNOT flag propagation.
